units.name: AI Literacy & Ethics (Level 6)
units.description: Rational agent frameworks, problem solving, and ethical algorithmic constraints.

questions.text: Scenario: A tech firm in Kilimani deploys an automated M-Pesa transaction monitoring agent. The agent must detect anomalous withdrawal patterns across millions of daily records. What fundamental AI component defines the measurable criteria by which this agent's success is judged?
questions.hint: Think of the quantitative benchmark that determines whether the agent is performing its designated task effectively.

options.text: Performance measure specifying fraud detection accuracy and false-positive thresholds
The agent's internal CPU clock speed during batch processing
The color scheme of the dashboard visualization interface
The number of software developers assigned to the project team

questions.text: Scenario: During a Nairobi traffic optimization pilot, an intelligent signal controller perceives vehicle density through induction loops embedded in road tarmac. In the PEAS framework, these induction loops are classified as:
questions.hint: PEAS categorizes components by function. Consider what role environmental detection mechanisms play in agent architecture.

options.text: Sensors that capture raw environmental state data for the agent's percept sequence
Actuators that physically rotate the traffic signal heads
Performance measures tracking average intersection wait times
Environment variables representing pedestrian crossing behaviors

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi hospital deploys an AI triage agent that routes emergency patients based on symptom severity. The agent operates in an environment where patient arrivals are continuous, the state space is partially observable due to incomplete medical histories, and each routing decision affects future bed availability. Why is this environment correctly classified as sequential rather than episodic?
questions.hint: Consider how current decisions alter the state space and influence the agent's future action possibilities.

options.text: Because each patient admission changes hospital resource availability, affecting subsequent triage decisions
Because the agent processes patients in discrete hourly batches with no inter-temporal dependencies
Because the environment is fully observable through the hospital's electronic records system
Because the agent resets its internal memory after every single patient interaction

questions.text: Scenario: A model-based reflex agent managing Kenya Power grid load balancing maintains an internal state representation of transformer temperatures and line voltages that are not directly sensed at every timestep. What is the primary purpose of this internal state model?
questions.hint: Reflect on why an agent would maintain historical or inferred information about environmental variables it cannot currently perceive.

options.text: To track unobserved aspects of the environment using stored knowledge about how the world evolves
To replace the need for physical sensors entirely and reduce hardware costs
To generate random predictions about future consumer electricity demand
To permanently store all historical data for annual audit compliance only

questions.text: Scenario: A goal-based agent is optimizing matatu route assignments across Nairobi's CBD during rush hour. The agent must choose between minimizing average passenger wait time versus minimizing total fuel consumption. Given conflicting objectives, which architectural enhancement allows the agent to resolve trade-offs systematically?
questions.hint: When an agent faces multiple competing objectives, what framework enables quantified preference ordering over outcomes?

options.text: A utility-based agent architecture that assigns numerical values to state outcomes and maximizes expected utility
A simple reflex agent that randomly selects routes to distribute traffic evenly
A model-based agent that only tracks current road congestion without preference modeling
A learning agent that waits for human dispatchers to manually resolve all conflicts

questions.text: Scenario: An autonomous cargo drone delivering medical supplies to a rural clinic in Machakos encounters unexpected terrain fog that degrades its camera sensors. The drone must decide whether to proceed using degraded visual data, hover until visibility improves, or return to base. Which agent characteristic is being tested?
questions.hint: Consider what property allows an agent to select appropriate actions when its perceptual inputs are incomplete or unreliable.

options.text: Rationality under perceptual uncertainty, where the agent maximizes expected performance given available information
Deterministic behavior that always follows the pre-programmed flight path regardless of conditions
Omniscience requiring complete knowledge of all future weather patterns
Random action selection to avoid predictable flight trajectories

questions.text: Scenario: A learning agent deployed at the Port of Mombasa container terminal initially performs poorly at scheduling ship offloading. Over six months, it analyzes historical berthing data, weather delays, and crane maintenance logs to improve its scheduling decisions. What specific learning paradigm is demonstrated when the agent uses labeled historical schedules marked as 'efficient' or 'inefficient' by human port managers?
questions.hint: Identify the machine learning category where training data includes explicit correct answers or target labels.

options.text: Supervised learning, where the agent learns from input-output pairs with known correct classifications
Unsupervised learning discovering hidden patterns without any human-provided efficiency labels
Reinforcement learning through trial-and-error with only delayed reward signals from ship captains
Transfer learning importing scheduling models from an unrelated airport baggage handling system

questions.text: Scenario: A multi-agent system coordinates ride-hailing vehicles across Nairobi during a sudden rainstorm surge. Agent A (a Bolt driver in Westlands) must decide whether to accept a passenger request in Karen while considering that Agent B (a competing driver) is also evaluating the same request. The environment exhibits which critical multi-agent property?
questions.hint: Examine how the strategic interdependence between competing agents transforms the decision space beyond single-agent optimization.

options.text: Competitive multi-agent environment where each agent's optimal strategy depends on predicting other agents' actions, creating a non-stationary policy landscape
Fully cooperative environment where all drivers share identical utility functions and pooled revenue
Single-agent deterministic environment where ride requests are pre-allocated by central dispatch without competition
Episodic environment where each ride request is completely independent of driver location and competitor behavior

questions.text: Scenario: An AI agent managing irrigation for a large-scale flower farm in Naivasha must operate in an environment where soil moisture sensors provide noisy readings, weather forecasts are probabilistic, and pump actuators have variable response delays. Analyze why this environment is simultaneously partially observable, stochastic, and dynamic.
questions.hint: Decompose the three environmental properties by mapping specific farm elements to each classification criterion.

options.text: Partially observable because sensor noise hides true soil state; stochastic because weather outcomes are probabilistic; dynamic because actuator delays and environmental changes occur while the agent deliberates

Fully observable because all farm variables are theoretically measurable with expensive sensors; deterministic because irrigation follows fixed physical laws; static because soil conditions never change
Partially observable because the farm manager occasionally overrides the agent; stochastic because flower prices fluctuate in Amsterdam auctions; dynamic because the agent reboots every midnight
Episodic because each irrigation cycle is independent; deterministic because water flow rates are constant; static because the farm layout never changes

questions.text: Scenario: A university in Eldoret deploys a simple reflex agent to control classroom lighting based solely on motion detection. During a lecture with minimal student movement, the lights repeatedly turn off, disrupting learning. Analyze the architectural limitation causing this failure and propose the minimal upgrade required.
questions.hint: Consider what information the simple reflex agent ignores that would prevent premature shutdown during low-motion academic activities.

options.text: The simple reflex agent lacks internal state to track whether a lecture is scheduled; upgrading to a model-based reflex agent with a time-table state model would resolve the issue
The motion sensors are too sensitive and should be replaced with thermal imaging cameras costing fifty thousand shillings each
The agent needs quantum computing hardware to process the complex social dynamics of classroom behavior
The failure is caused by students using mobile phones instead of taking notes, which is outside the agent's control domain

assessments.name: CAT Element 2: Problem Solving & Search Algorithms

questions.text: Scenario: A logistics company in Nakuru uses Breadth-First Search to find the shortest delivery route from their depot to a new retail outlet. BFS explores all nodes at the present depth before moving to nodes at the next depth level. What data structure fundamentally enables this level-by-level exploration pattern?
questions.hint: Consider the abstract data structure that processes elements in the exact order they were discovered, ensuring shallowest nodes are expanded first.

options.text: A First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue that enqueues newly discovered nodes at the rear and dequeues from the front
A Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack that pushes and pops nodes from the same end
A binary search tree ordered by node heuristic values
A hash map with constant-time lookup for visited node states

questions.text: Scenario: An A* search algorithm is guiding an emergency response vehicle through Nairobi's road network to Kenyatta National Hospital. The algorithm uses Euclidean distance as its heuristic function. For A* to guarantee finding the optimal shortest path, what mathematical property must this heuristic satisfy?
questions.hint: Recall the formal constraint on heuristic estimates that ensures they never exceed the true remaining cost to the goal.

options.text: Admissibility, meaning the heuristic never overestimates the actual cost from any node to the goal
Monotonicity requiring the heuristic to increase at every search step
Completeness ensuring the heuristic explores every node in the graph
Consistency demanding the heuristic value equals zero at all non-goal nodes

questions.text: Scenario: A Depth-First Search algorithm is exploring possible supply chain configurations for a tea export company in Kericho. The search tree has extremely deep branches representing multi-month procurement sequences. Why might DFS fail to find any valid configuration even if one exists?
questions.hint: Consider what happens when DFS follows a single path that extends infinitely or cyclically without ever exploring alternative branches.

options.text: DFS is not complete in infinite-depth spaces because it may follow a single infinite path forever without backtracking to explore alternatives
DFS always finds the optimal solution but requires exponential memory to store the entire search tree
DFS fails because it requires a perfectly balanced binary tree structure to operate correctly
DFS cannot handle supply chain problems because they violate the graph coloring constraint

questions.text: Scenario: In a university timetabling system for JKUAT, a constraint satisfaction problem assigns lecturers to rooms and time slots. The 'all-different' constraint ensures no lecturer is scheduled in two rooms simultaneously. What does this constraint specifically enforce about the variable assignments?
questions.hint: Think about what mathematical property the all-different constraint imposes on the values assigned to a set of variables.

options.text: Each variable in the constrained set must be assigned a unique value distinct from all other variables in that set
All variables must be assigned the identical value to maintain scheduling uniformity
Variables may take any value as long as the sum of all assignments equals the total number of rooms
Each variable assignment must be a prime number to ensure computational efficiency

questions.text: Scenario: A matatu SACCO in Eastleigh needs to optimize routes across 15 pickup points using a heuristic search. Greedy Best-First Search always expands the node that appears closest to the destination based on straight-line distance. Calculate the risk: if the straight-line distance heuristic leads the search into a narrow one-way street with a dead-end, what is the algorithm's fundamental weakness?
questions.hint: Analyze why an algorithm that ignores the cost already incurred might commit to paths that appear promising locally but fail globally.

options.text: Greedy search lacks memory of accumulated path cost, making it susceptible to local traps and unable to backtrack when the heuristic proves deceptive
Greedy search requires too much memory to store the entire route map of Nairobi
Greedy search cannot handle one-way streets because it violates the bidirectional search requirement
Greedy search always finds the optimal route but takes too long to compute during rush hour

questions.text: Scenario: A water distribution network in Kisumu is modeled as a graph where nodes represent junctions and edges represent pipes with flow capacities. The city engineer needs to determine the maximum water flow from the main reservoir to the eastern suburbs. Which classical algorithmic problem does this directly map to?
questions.hint: Identify the well-known network flow problem that maximizes throughput from a single source to a single sink in a capacitated directed graph.

options.text: The Maximum Flow problem, solvable using algorithms like Ford-Fulkerson or Edmonds-Karp
The Traveling Salesman Problem seeking the shortest tour visiting all junctions
The Knapsack Problem optimizing pipe material selection within a budget constraint
The PageRank algorithm ranking junction importance by random water molecule walks

questions.text: Scenario: An A* search is finding the optimal path for an ambulance from Karen to Nairobi Hospital. The evaluation function is f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the actual distance traveled so far and h(n) is the estimated remaining distance. At a particular node, g(n) = 8.2 km and h(n) = 3.1 km. A neighboring node has g(n) = 9.5 km and h(n) = 1.8 km. Which node will A* prioritize and why?
questions.hint: Compute the f(n) values for both nodes and identify which evaluation score indicates a more promising path toward the goal.

options.text: The current node with f(n) = 11.3 km is prioritized over the neighbor with f(n) = 11.3 km; both have equal f-scores and tie-breaking rules apply
The neighbor with f(n) = 9.5 km is prioritized because lower g(n) always indicates a better path
The current node is abandoned because h(n) = 3.1 km exceeds the admissibility threshold
A* randomly selects between nodes when their f-scores are equal to encourage exploration diversity

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan e-commerce platform uses uniform-cost search to find the cheapest shipping route from Mombasa to a customer in Kakamega. The algorithm maintains a priority queue ordered by path cost. Analyze why uniform-cost search is guaranteed to find the optimal solution in this scenario, and identify its primary computational drawback compared to BFS.
questions.hint: Consider the optimality proof based on path cost expansion ordering, then contrast the memory requirements when edge costs vary versus when they are uniform.

options.text: Uniform-cost search expands nodes in order of increasing path cost, guaranteeing the first goal node reached has minimum cost; its drawback is potentially exploring many high-cost paths before finding the optimal low-cost solution, consuming significant memory
Uniform-cost search is optimal because it uses a random shuffle to avoid local minima; its drawback is requiring quantum computing for large graphs
Uniform-cost search is not guaranteed optimal because it ignores heuristic information about shipping distances
Uniform-cost search is identical to BFS in all respects including memory usage and optimality conditions

questions.text: Scenario: A university AI research group is comparing iterative deepening search (IDS) against standard depth-first search for exploring game move trees in a Kenyan chess engine. IDS repeatedly applies DFS with increasing depth limits. Analyze the space complexity advantage of IDS and explain why it maintains DFS's completeness in finite spaces.
questions.hint: Compare the linear space complexity of depth-limited DFS with the exponential space of BFS, while noting how iterative deepening ensures all depths are eventually explored.

options.text: IDS has O(bd) space complexity matching DFS because it stores only the current path, while completeness is maintained because increasing depth limits eventually reach any finite-depth goal node
IDS has O(b^d) space complexity like BFS because it stores all previously explored nodes across iterations
IDS is incomplete in finite spaces because depth limits prevent exploration beyond the maximum iteration bound
IDS requires O(d!) space because each iteration factorially increases the branching factor

questions.text: Scenario: A bi-directional search is deployed to find the shortest meeting point between two courier vans: one departing from Nairobi CBD and another from Thika town. The algorithm searches simultaneously from both start nodes toward each other. Analyze the theoretical time and space complexity improvement over uni-directional BFS, and state the critical requirement for this improvement to hold.
questions.hint: Consider how searching from both directions reduces the effective search depth, and identify what precondition about the search space topology enables the complexity reduction.

options.text: Bi-directional search reduces time and space complexity from O(b^d) to O(b^(d/2)) by meeting in the middle; the critical requirement is that the goal state is explicitly known and the search space is reversible
Bi-directional search has identical complexity to uni-directional search because both must explore the entire graph
Bi-directional search improves complexity only when the branching factor b equals exactly 2
Bi-directional search requires O(b^2d) space because it maintains two separate exponential frontiers

assessments.name: CAT Element 3: Logic Operators & Knowledge Predicates

questions.text: Scenario: A credit scoring AI at a Nairobi micro-finance institution evaluates loan applicants using logical rules. The system applies the rule: IF (applicant_has_collateral = TRUE) AND (credit_score > 650) THEN approve_loan. Which logical operator connects the two antecedent conditions?
questions.hint: Identify the Boolean operator that requires both conditions to be simultaneously true for the consequent to fire.

options.text: The logical conjunction AND, which evaluates to true only when both operands are true
The logical disjunction OR, which evaluates to true when at least one operand is true
The logical implication THEN, which reverses the truth value of the antecedent
The logical negation NOT, which inverts the truth value of the entire expression

questions.text: Scenario: In a propositional logic knowledge base for a Kenyan agricultural advisory system, the statement 'If soil_pH < 6.5 THEN apply_lime' is represented as P → Q. What is the logical contrapositive of this implication, and is it semantically equivalent?
questions.hint: Recall the formal transformation of an implication into its contrapositive form and whether truth tables confirm equivalence.

options.text: ¬Q → ¬P ('If do not apply lime then soil pH is not less than 6.5'), which is logically equivalent to the original implication
Q → P ('If apply lime then soil pH is less than 6.5'), which is the converse and not equivalent
P ∧ Q ('Soil pH is less than 6.5 AND apply lime'), which strengthens rather than transforms the implication
¬P ∨ Q ('Soil pH is not less than 6.5 OR apply lime'), which is the disjunctive normal form, not the contrapositive

questions.text: Scenario: A predicate logic system managing wildlife conservation in the Maasai Mara uses the predicate Protected(x) meaning 'species x is protected by law.' The statement ∀x (Endangered(x) → Protected(x)) is universally quantified. What does this statement formally assert?
questions.hint: Parse the universal quantifier and implication structure to determine what relationship holds between endangered status and legal protection.

options.text: For every species x, if x is endangered then x is protected by law; all endangered species are protected
There exists at least one endangered species that is protected; no claim about all endangered species
All protected species are necessarily endangered, reversing the logical dependency
No species can be both endangered and protected simultaneously, asserting mutual exclusivity

questions.text: Scenario: An expert system for Kenyan tax law uses first-order predicate logic to reason about business deductions. The knowledge base contains: Deductible(x) → ReducesTax(x); BusinessExpense(fuel_cost) → Deductible(fuel_cost); BusinessExpense(fuel_cost). Using modus ponens chaining, what can be inferred?
questions.hint: Trace the forward chaining of logical deductions: apply modus ponens to the ground facts and rules in sequence.

options.text: ReducesTax(fuel_cost) can be inferred by chaining: BusinessExpense(fuel_cost) implies Deductible(fuel_cost), which implies ReducesTax(fuel_cost)
BusinessExpense(fuel_cost) is the final inferred conclusion with no further deductions possible
Deductible(fuel_cost) is rejected because fuel costs are universally non-deductible in all jurisdictions
The system enters an infinite loop because modus ponens cannot terminate on recursive rules

questions.text: Scenario: A logical inference engine at a Kenyan bank must determine whether a loan applicant qualifies for a special rate. The rules are: (1) GoodCredit(x) ∧ StableIncome(x) → SpecialRate(x); (2) GoodCredit(Juma); (3) StableIncome(Juma). Apply forward chaining to determine if SpecialRate(Juma) can be derived.
questions.hint: Match the antecedent literals of rule 1 with the ground facts in the knowledge base to trigger the consequent.

options.text: SpecialRate(Juma) is derived because both GoodCredit(Juma) and StableIncome(Juma) are known facts that satisfy rule 1's antecedent
SpecialRate(Juma) cannot be derived because forward chaining only works with negated predicates
SpecialRate(Juma) is rejected because the rule requires OR rather than AND between the conditions
The inference engine crashes because Juma appears in multiple facts, causing a unification conflict

questions.text: Scenario: A resolution refutation system is proving that a Kenyan wildlife reserve is sustainable. The knowledge base contains clauses: ¬Poached(x) ∨ Endangered(x) and Poached(rhino). What resolvent is produced when applying the resolution rule to these two clauses?
questions.hint: Identify the complementary literals in the two clauses and apply the resolution inference rule to derive the resolvent.

options.text: Endangered(rhino), obtained by resolving ¬Poached(rhino) with Poached(rhino) and substituting x = rhino
¬Endangered(rhino), which is the negation of the expected conclusion
Poached(x) ∧ Endangered(x), which incorrectly conjoins rather than resolves the clauses
An empty clause indicating the knowledge base is inconsistent

questions.text: Scenario: A knowledge-based agent managing a Nairobi smart building uses the predicate Occupied(room, time) and the rule ∀r∀t (Occupied(r, t) → TurnOnLights(r, t)). The agent perceives Occupied(conference_room, 14:00). Using generalized modus ponens with unification, what action is inferred?
questions.hint: Apply unification to match the perceived fact with the rule's antecedent, then instantiate the consequent with the unified substitutions.

options.text: TurnOnLights(conference_room, 14:00) is inferred by unifying r with conference_room and t with 14:00
Occupied(conference_room, 14:00) is re-inferred as a tautology with no new information
TurnOffLights(conference_room, 14:00) is inferred by negating the rule's consequent
The unification fails because conference_room is a constant and cannot substitute the variable r

questions.text: Scenario: An AI system auditing Kenyan public procurement contracts detects a logical inconsistency in the constraint set: (A) All contracts over KES 10M require board approval; (B) Contract X is valued at KES 15M; (C) Contract X did not receive board approval. Using resolution refutation, analyze how the system proves inconsistency.
questions.hint: Formalize the natural language statements as clauses, negate the query, and trace the resolution steps that derive the empty clause.

options.text: The system formalizes: ¬Over10M(x) ∨ BoardApproval(x); Over10M(X); ¬BoardApproval(X). Resolving the first two yields BoardApproval(X), which resolves with ¬BoardApproval(X) to produce the empty clause, proving inconsistency
The system concludes the knowledge base is consistent because three statements cannot logically contradict each other
The system applies fuzzy logic to assign a 0.7 truth value to the inconsistency claim
The system requires a human auditor because automated resolution cannot handle monetary values

questions.text: Scenario: A backward-chaining expert system for Kenyan medical diagnosis starts with the goal Diagnosed(patient, malaria) and works backward through rules. The rule base contains: Fever(x) ∧ Headache(x) ∧ Chills(x) → Malaria(x); RapidTestPositive(x) → Malaria(x). Given Fever(Juma), Headache(Juma), and RapidTestPositive(Juma), analyze why backward chaining is efficient here.
questions.hint: Consider how backward chaining focuses only on rules relevant to the goal, avoiding exploration of irrelevant medical conditions.

options.text: Backward chaining starts from the goal and only explores rules that could prove Malaria(x), directly checking if Fever, Headache, Chills or RapidTestPositive hold for Juma without exploring unrelated disease rules
Backward chaining is inefficient because it must evaluate all possible diseases before narrowing to malaria
Backward chaining cannot handle multiple rules with the same consequent because it causes infinite recursion
Backward chaining requires converting all rules to disjunctive normal form before execution

questions.text: Scenario: A first-order logic knowledge base for a Kenyan railway scheduling system contains the statement ∃x (Train(x) ∧ Delayed(x) ∧ Route(x, nairobi_mombasa)). A Skolemization preprocessing step is applied for resolution-based theorem proving. Analyze what Skolemization produces and why it preserves satisfiability.
questions.hint: Recall how existential quantifiers are eliminated by introducing Skolem constants or functions, and why this transformation is satisfiability-preserving.

options.text: Skolemization replaces ∃x with a Skolem constant c, yielding Train(c) ∧ Delayed(c) ∧ Route(c, nairobi_mombasa); this preserves satisfiability because if the original is satisfiable, some specific individual satisfies it, and c represents that witness
Skolemization removes all predicates and replaces them with propositional variables, losing expressive power
Skolemization universally quantifies all variables, converting the statement to ∀x (Train(x) ∧ ...)
Skolemization proves the statement is a tautology by exhaustive truth table enumeration

assessments.name: CAT Element 4: Machine Learning Frameworks & Bias

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi fintech startup trains a logistic regression model to predict loan default risk using applicant income, employment history, and credit bureau scores. During training, the model minimizes a specific loss function. What is the canonical loss function optimized by logistic regression for binary classification?
questions.hint: Recall the probabilistic loss measure that penalizes confident wrong predictions more heavily than uncertain ones in binary classification.

options.text: Binary cross-entropy loss (log loss), which measures the divergence between predicted probabilities and true binary labels
Mean squared error, which computes the squared difference between predicted probabilities and class labels
Hinge loss, which is primarily used in support vector machine formulations
Kullback-Leibler divergence between the input feature distributions and a standard normal prior

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan agricultural AI system classifies crop diseases from leaf images using a convolutional neural network. The output layer produces raw logit scores [2.1, 0.5, -1.3] for three disease classes. Which activation function converts these logits into a valid probability distribution?
questions.hint: Identify the function that exponentiates and normalizes a vector of real numbers into probabilities summing to exactly 1.

options.text: Softmax function, computing exp(z_i) / sum(exp(z_j)) for each class i
Sigmoid function, which independently maps each logit to a value between 0 and 1 without normalization
ReLU activation, which zeroes negative logits and passes positive values unchanged
Tanh function, which squashes logits to the range [-1, 1] without probability interpretation

questions.text: Scenario: A mobile lending app in Kilimani observes that their loan approval model achieves 98% accuracy on the training dataset but only 62% accuracy on a held-out test set of new applicants. What machine learning pathology does this performance gap indicate?
questions.hint: Consider the condition where a model memorizes training data patterns including noise, failing to generalize to unseen examples.

options.text: Overfitting, where the model captures training-specific noise and loses generalization capability on new data
Underfitting, where the model is too simple to capture even the training data patterns
Data leakage, where test set information was accidentally included in the training pipeline
Concept drift, where the underlying data distribution changed between training and testing periods

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan hospital deploys a pneumonia detection model trained predominantly on chest X-rays from European populations. When deployed in Nairobi, the model's sensitivity drops significantly for Kenyan patients. What type of algorithmic bias is primarily responsible?
questions.hint: Analyze how the training data's demographic composition differs from the deployment population and what bias category this mismatch creates.

options.text: Representation bias, where the training data under-represents the demographic characteristics of the target deployment population
Measurement bias, where the X-ray imaging equipment in Nairobi produces systematically different pixel values
Aggregation bias, where a single model is inappropriately applied to multiple distinct disease subtypes
Evaluation bias, where the wrong performance metric was selected for the clinical context

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi insurance company uses a K-Nearest Neighbors classifier with K=5 to categorize motor vehicle claims as fraudulent or legitimate. A new claim arrives with feature vector [age=35, claim_amount=45000, policy_tenure=3]. The 5 nearest neighbors in the training set are: 3 fraudulent, 2 legitimate. What is KNN's prediction and what voting mechanism produces it?
questions.hint: Apply the majority voting rule among the K nearest neighbors to determine the predicted class label.

options.text: Fraudulent, determined by majority vote where 3 out of 5 nearest neighbors are fraudulent
Legitimate, determined by averaging the continuous feature distances rather than class labels
Fraudulent with probability 0.6, but KNN requires K to be an even number for tie-breaking
The prediction is undefined because claim_amount is a continuous variable incompatible with KNN

questions.text: Scenario: A Naive Bayes classifier is trained on Swahili news articles to categorize them as politics, sports, or entertainment. The model computes P(class|words) using Bayes' theorem with the conditional independence assumption. Given P(sports)=0.3, P('goal'|sports)=0.15, and P('goal'|not sports)=0.02, calculate how the presence of 'goal' updates the odds in favor of sports.
questions.hint: Compute the likelihood ratio P('goal'|sports) / P('goal'|not sports) and multiply by the prior odds to obtain posterior odds.

options.text: The likelihood ratio is 7.5 (0.15/0.02), multiplying prior odds 0.3/0.7 by 7.5 yields posterior odds of approximately 3.21 in favor of sports
The posterior probability is 0.15 * 0.3 = 0.045, which is below the 0.5 threshold for sports classification
The likelihood ratio is 0.15 + 0.02 = 0.17, which is insufficient to change the classification decision
Naive Bayes cannot handle the word 'goal' because it is not in the training vocabulary

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan telco builds a churn prediction model using a decision tree. The tree splits customers on 'monthly_data_usage <= 5GB' at the root node. The information gain for this split is 0.45 bits. The next best split on 'customer_tenure <= 12 months' yields information gain of 0.38 bits. Why does the algorithm prefer the data usage split?
questions.hint: Consider how information gain quantifies the reduction in entropy (uncertainty) about the target variable after a split.

options.text: The data usage split provides greater entropy reduction (0.45 > 0.38), meaning it separates churned from retained customers more effectively
Data usage is measured in gigabytes which are larger units than months, so the split is numerically superior
The algorithm randomly selects between splits with information gain above 0.3, and data usage was evaluated first
Customer tenure is a protected attribute under data privacy law, so the algorithm automatically rejects it

questions.text: Scenario: A facial recognition system deployed at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport exhibits higher false positive rates for passengers with dark skin tones compared to light skin tones. The training dataset contained 85% light-skinned faces. Analyze the compounding factors: how do dataset imbalance, feature representation, and evaluation metric selection collectively produce this disparate impact?
questions.hint: Decompose the bias pipeline: consider how class imbalance affects model optimization, how underrepresented features are learned, and how aggregate accuracy metrics mask subgroup disparities.

options.text: Dataset imbalance causes the model to optimize for the majority class; underrepresented dark-skinned features are poorly learned; aggregate accuracy metrics conceal subgroup performance gaps, producing higher false positives for the minority group
The airport lighting is insufficient for dark skin tones, which is a hardware issue unrelated to algorithmic bias
False positive rates are mathematically impossible to equalize across demographic groups due to the curse of dimensionality
The model is intentionally biased because the airport security team requested higher scrutiny for certain passenger profiles

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi credit scoring startup uses a random forest ensemble to predict loan defaults. Each tree in the forest is trained on a bootstrap sample of the data. Analyze how this bagging procedure reduces variance compared to a single decision tree, and explain why random feature subsets at each split further decorrelate the trees.
questions.hint: Consider how averaging multiple noisy but unbiased estimators reduces variance, and how restricting features at each split prevents all trees from making the same early splits on dominant features.

options.text: Bagging reduces variance by averaging predictions from trees trained on different data subsets; random feature subsets prevent all trees from selecting the same strongest predictor early, increasing ensemble diversity and reducing correlation between trees
Bagging increases variance by introducing randomness that amplifies prediction errors across the ensemble
Random feature subsets are unnecessary because decision trees are already uncorrelated by nature
The variance reduction comes solely from pruning individual trees, not from the ensemble aggregation mechanism

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan agricultural extension service deploys a neural network to recommend fertilizer types based on soil composition. The model was trained on data from large-scale commercial farms in Nakuru but is now being used by smallholder farmers in Kitui with very different soil profiles. Analyze the technical and ethical dimensions of this transfer, including concept drift, domain adaptation needs, and potential harm to vulnerable farmers.
questions.hint: Examine the technical gap between training and deployment distributions, the need for domain adaptation techniques, and the ethical responsibility when algorithmic errors could harm economically vulnerable users.

options.text: Concept drift between Nakuru and Kitui soil profiles degrades model accuracy; domain adaptation through transfer learning or retraining on local data is needed; deploying without validation risks recommending wrong fertilizers, causing crop failure and financial harm to smallholders
The model will perform identically across regions because neural networks are universally generalizable
Smallholder farmers should not use AI tools because they lack the technical expertise to interpret recommendations
The ethical concern is irrelevant because fertilizer recommendations are always harmless regardless of soil type

questions.text: Scenario: An autonomous matatu fare collection agent in Nairobi uses PEAS to model its decision environment. The 'Performance' component specifically measures: (a) total revenue collected, (b) passenger satisfaction ratings, and (c) compliance with NTSA regulations. What type of performance measure architecture is this?
questions.hint: Consider how multiple evaluation criteria are combined when an agent must optimize across several objectives simultaneously.

options.text: A multi-objective performance measure requiring trade-off analysis between revenue, satisfaction, and compliance

EMV = max(500K, 200K, -100K) = 500K KES, assuming the best case always occurs

questions.text: Scenario: A multi-agent system models Nairobi's matatu industry where individual drivers (agents) compete for passengers along shared routes. Each driver has private information about passenger demand at their current location. Analyze how the system exhibits emergent behavior: how do local greedy decisions by individual drivers produce global traffic patterns?
questions.hint: Consider how local optimization (drivers choosing the most profitable routes) can lead to globally suboptimal outcomes (traffic congestion, oversupply on popular routes).

options.text: Individual drivers greedily choose high-demand routes, causing oversupply and congestion on those routes while underserved areas remain neglected; this emergent pattern resembles the tragedy of the commons and requires coordination mechanisms or regulatory intervention
Individual drivers always make globally optimal decisions because local profit maximization aligns with social welfare
The system cannot exhibit emergent behavior because matatu drivers do not use AI algorithms
Traffic patterns are predetermined by the Nairobi city planning department and unaffected by driver behavior

questions.text: Scenario: A bidirectional search finds the shortest path between two Mombasa port terminals. The forward search from Terminal A and backward search from Terminal B meet at an intermediate node. What is the theoretical time complexity improvement over uni-directional BFS?
questions.hint: Recall the complexity reduction from O(b^d) to O(b^(d/2)) when searching from both directions simultaneously.

options.text: The complexity improves from O(b^d) to O(b^(d/2)), a dramatic reduction because the searches meet in the middle
The complexity worsens to O(2b^d) because two searches consume twice the resources
The complexity remains O(b^d) because meeting in the middle does not reduce the effective search depth
The complexity becomes O(d^b), which is polynomial in the branching factor

questions.text: Scenario: A constraint satisfaction problem for Kenyan nurse scheduling uses arc consistency (AC-3) to prune domains. After assigning Nurse A to the morning shift, arc consistency checks all arcs between unassigned variables. What does it mean for an arc (X, Y) to be consistent?
questions.hint: Recall the definition of arc consistency: for every value in X's domain, there must exist a supporting value in Y's domain.

options.text: For every value x in X's domain, there exists at least one value y in Y's domain such that the constraint between X and Y is satisfied
X and Y have identical domains after pruning, ensuring perfect symmetry in the schedule
The arc is consistent if X has more remaining values than Y, indicating greater scheduling flexibility
Arc consistency requires that X and Y are assigned to the same shift to maintain workforce balance

questions.text: Scenario: A minimax algorithm with alpha-beta pruning plays a Kenyan strategy game. The game tree has depth 4, branching factor 3. Without pruning, minimax evaluates 3^4 = 81 leaf nodes. With perfect move ordering, how many leaf nodes does alpha-beta evaluate?
questions.hint: With perfect ordering, alpha-beta evaluates O(b^(d/2)) leaf nodes for even depth, approximately the square root of the total nodes.

options.text: Approximately 3^(4/2) = 9 leaf nodes, a reduction from 81 to about 9 with perfect ordering
Exactly 81 leaf nodes because alpha-beta pruning does not reduce the number of evaluations
0 leaf nodes because alpha-beta terminates immediately without evaluating any leaves
4 × 3 = 12 leaf nodes, multiplying depth by branching factor

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan delivery company uses Dijkstra's algorithm to find shortest paths in a road network where edge weights represent travel time in minutes. A particular road segment has weight 15. After a traffic accident, the weight increases to 45. How does Dijkstra's algorithm handle this dynamic weight change if already executed?
questions.hint: Standard Dijkstra assumes static weights; consider what happens when the graph changes after the algorithm has computed shortest paths.

options.text: Standard Dijkstra does not handle dynamic changes; the algorithm must be re-executed with the updated weights, or a dynamic shortest path algorithm like DynDijkstra must be used
Dijkstra automatically detects weight changes and updates all paths in constant time without re-execution
Dijkstra ignores the weight change because it only processes positive weights, not weight increases
Dijkstra crashes when any edge weight changes because its priority queue becomes corrupted

questions.text: Scenario: A genetic algorithm optimizes the layout of a Kenyan supermarket to maximize customer flow and product exposure. The chromosome encodes shelf positions for 50 product categories. After 100 generations, the population converges to similar layouts with minor variations. Analyze whether this convergence indicates finding the global optimum or premature convergence, and propose diagnostic tests.
questions.hint: Distinguish between healthy convergence to a good solution and premature convergence to a local optimum; consider diversity metrics and fitness landscape analysis.

options.text: Convergence with minor variations may indicate either finding a good optimum or premature convergence; diagnostic tests include measuring population diversity (should remain above threshold), running multiple independent runs with different seeds, and analyzing fitness landscape ruggedness to distinguish global basins from local traps
Convergence always indicates finding the global optimum because genetic algorithms are guaranteed global optimizers
Convergence always indicates premature convergence and the algorithm has failed completely
The only diagnostic test is to increase the population size to 10,000 chromosomes regardless of the problem

questions.text: Scenario: In propositional logic, the statement ¬(P ∨ Q) is logically equivalent to which compound statement by De Morgan's laws?
questions.hint: Apply De Morgan's law that negates a disjunction by negating each disjunct and converting to a conjunction.

options.text: ¬P ∧ ¬Q, by De Morgan's law: the negation of a disjunction is the conjunction of the negations
¬P ∨ ¬Q, which incorrectly maintains the disjunction connective
P ∧ Q, which removes all negations rather than distributing them
P ∨ Q, which is the original statement without any negation

questions.text: Scenario: A first-order logic knowledge base for Kenyan wildlife contains the sentence ∀x (Predator(x) → ∃y (Prey(y) ∧ Hunts(x, y))). What does this sentence assert about the relationship between predators and prey?
questions.hint: Parse the nested quantifiers: universal over predators, existential over prey, with a conjunction linking hunting behavior.

options.text: For every predator x, there exists some prey y such that x hunts y; every predator has at least one prey species
There exists a single prey species that all predators hunt collectively
Every prey is hunted by every predator, a universal relationship in both directions
Predators and prey are mutually exclusive categories with no hunting relationship

questions.text: Scenario: A forward chaining system in a Kenyan banking expert system has the following rules: (1) SavingsAccount(x) → LowRisk(x); (2) LowRisk(x) → Approved(x); (3) SavingsAccount(Wanjiku). What is the complete chain of inferred conclusions?
questions.hint: Apply modus ponens iteratively: use fact (3) with rule (1), then use the result with rule (2).

options.text: From (3) and (1): LowRisk(Wanjiku). From LowRisk(Wanjiku) and (2): Approved(Wanjiku). Complete chain: SavingsAccount → LowRisk → Approved.
Only Approved(Wanjiku) is inferred because forward chaining skips intermediate conclusions
Only LowRisk(Wanjiku) is inferred because rule (2) requires additional evidence not provided
No conclusions are inferred because Wanjiku is a constant and cannot substitute for variable x

questions.text: Scenario: A resolution theorem prover in a Kenyan legal system is asked to prove Liability(CompanyX) from: (1) Negligent(x) → Liability(x); (2) ViolatedSafety(x) → Negligent(x); (3) ViolatedSafety(CompanyX). Show the resolution steps.
questions.hint: Convert implications to clauses, negate the goal, and resolve step by step until the empty clause is derived.

options.text: Clauses: ¬Negligent(x) ∨ Liability(x); ¬ViolatedSafety(x) ∨ Negligent(x); ViolatedSafety(CompanyX). Negate goal: ¬Liability(CompanyX). Resolve clause 1 with negated goal: ¬Negligent(CompanyX). Resolve with clause 2: ¬ViolatedSafety(CompanyX). Resolve with clause 3: Empty clause. QED.
Resolution fails because the knowledge base contains only implications, not disjunctions
The proof requires converting to decimal arithmetic before resolution can proceed
Liability(CompanyX) is rejected because the company has not been proven negligent beyond reasonable doubt

questions.text: Scenario: A description logic ontology for Kenyan healthcare classifies diseases and symptoms. The ontology uses concept inclusion axioms: Malaria ⊑ Fever ⊓ Headache ⊓ Chills. A patient is diagnosed with Fever, Headache, and Fatigue (but not Chills). Analyze the inference: can the system conclude Malaria? What is the open-world vs. closed-world assumption issue?
questions.hint: Consider how the open-world assumption in DL treats missing information as unknown rather than false, affecting subsumption inference.

options.text: Under the open-world assumption, the system cannot conclude Malaria because the absence of Chills is not evidence against Malaria (the patient might have unobserved Chills); under closed-world assumption, the absence would be treated as negation, potentially allowing the inference
The system can conclude Malaria because Fever and Headache are sufficient conditions under the ontology definition
The system rejects the diagnosis because the patient has Fatigue, which is not in the Malaria definition
Description logic cannot handle patient-specific instances and only works with abstract disease categories

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan agricultural AI uses a support vector machine with an RBF kernel to classify crop stress levels from drone imagery. The regularization parameter C controls the trade-off between margin width and classification error. What happens when C approaches infinity?
questions.hint: Consider how C penalizes misclassification; as C increases, the penalty for training errors becomes severe.

options.text: The SVM seeks a hyperplane with zero training error, potentially overfitting by allowing a very narrow margin
The SVM ignores all training errors and maximizes margin width regardless of classification accuracy
The SVM automatically switches to a linear kernel because RBF is incompatible with large C values
The SVM's decision boundary becomes a perfect circle enclosing all training data points

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan hospital's pneumonia detection CNN achieves 96% accuracy on X-rays from Nairobi patients but only 74% on patients from rural Western Kenya. The training data is 90% from Nairobi. What data-centric intervention most directly addresses this performance gap?
questions.hint: Consider how the training data distribution mismatch causes the performance gap, and what data collection strategy would most directly improve rural performance.

options.text: Collecting and incorporating more X-rays from rural Western Kenya into the training dataset to improve representation of that demographic
Increasing the number of convolutional layers in the CNN architecture
Reducing the learning rate by a factor of 10 during training
Replacing the CNN with a decision tree classifier

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi stock prediction model uses a gradient boosting regressor (XGBoost) with 1000 estimators. The learning rate is 0.05. The model's training RMSE is 2.3 and validation RMSE is 8.7. Which hyperparameter adjustment most directly addresses the indicated overfitting?
questions.hint: Consider regularization techniques in gradient boosting: reducing model complexity, increasing regularization, or adjusting the learning rate.

options.text: Reducing the number of estimators to 200 and increasing the learning rate to 0.1, or adding subsampling and regularization parameters like lambda and alpha
Increasing estimators to 5000 and reducing learning rate to 0.01 to fit the training data more closely
Removing all regularization and allowing the model to memorize the training data perfectly
Switching to a linear regression model because gradient boosting is inherently flawed

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan bank's credit scoring model uses a neural network with 3 hidden layers. The bank must explain loan denial decisions to regulators under the Kenyan Data Protection Act. The network's weights are not directly interpretable. What technique provides post-hoc explanations by approximating the model locally with an interpretable surrogate?
questions.hint: Identify the technique that trains a simple, interpretable model (like linear regression or decision tree) to approximate the complex model's predictions in the neighborhood of a specific instance.

options.text: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), which fits a local linear model around the prediction to explain feature contributions
Backpropagation, which computes gradients for training but does not provide human-interpretable explanations
Dropout, which is a regularization technique for preventing overfitting during training
One-hot encoding, which converts categorical variables to binary vectors for neural network input

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan government deploys an AI system to allocate public housing in Nairobi. The system uses historical data where certain ethnic neighborhoods were historically underfunded. The model learns to predict 'high risk' for applicants from these neighborhoods, perpetuating historical discrimination. Analyze the full ethical pipeline: data collection bias, feature proxy discrimination, feedback loops, and corrective interventions.
questions.hint: Trace the bias from historical data through feature engineering to deployment outcomes, and consider technical and policy interventions at each stage.

options.text: Historical underfunding creates representation bias in training data; neighborhood features act as proxies for ethnicity, enabling indirect discrimination; feedback loops reinforce the bias as denials become training data; interventions include removing proxy features, reweighting training data, adversarial debiasing, and establishing human oversight with appeals processes
The system is ethically neutral because it uses objective historical data without human prejudice
The bias is caused by applicants from these neighborhoods genuinely having worse creditworthiness
AI systems should not be used for public housing allocation because algorithms are inherently racist

questions.text: Scenario: An administrative assistant at a Nairobi law firm connects a new biometric fingerprint scanner to the front desk computer via USB. The device powers on but Windows displays 'Unknown Device' in Device Manager. What is the missing system component?

SSDs use larger magnetic platters that spin at 15,000 RPM compared to HDDs' 7,200 RPM
SSDs store data in sequential blocks only, eliminating the need for file fragmentation management

Microsoft Word's Document Inspector, which checks for hidden metadata in patient record files
The Windows Registry Editor, which stores hardware configuration but does not display real-time usage
The Command Prompt, which only executes batch scripts and cannot display system resources

Share the administrator password with all staff members to ensure anyone can install software at any time

questions.hint: Identify the mechanism that groups users by role and assigns permissions to resources based on group membership rather than individual accounts.

Organizational Units, which only control desktop wallpaper and screensaver policies
Domain Controllers, which authenticate users but do not manage file-level permissions
Global Catalogs, which only store directory information for cross-domain searches

questions.text: Scenario: A Thika manufacturing plant's administrative office experiences frequent power outages. The IT manager configures all workstations to automatically save documents to a network drive every 5 minutes. Which operating system feature enables this automated backup behavior?
questions.hint: Consider the OS component that schedules and executes repetitive tasks at specified intervals without user intervention.

options.text: Task Scheduler (Windows) or cron (Linux), which executes scripts or applications at predefined time intervals
The Recycle Bin, which automatically backs up deleted files to network storage
The Clipboard Manager, which saves copied text to a network database every 5 minutes
The BIOS Power Management settings, which control hardware sleep timers but not file operations

Immediately reformat the hard drive without investigation, losing all procurement records
Disconnect the computer from power and wait 24 hours for the malware to expire naturally

questions.hint: Consider which file systems both OSes can natively read/write, and which network protocols provide transparent file access across platforms.

APFS (Apple File System) is the only cross-compatible file system for Windows and Linux

Windows 7 is more secure than Windows 11 because older systems have fewer features to exploit

The hospital should switch to macOS because Apple computers are immune to malware

Owner: read+write+execute (rwx); Group: read+write (rw-); Others: read only (r--)

Owner: full access (777); Group: no access (---); Others: no access (---)

Grant Everyone Full Control and trust employees not to delete files based on office policy

The file is permanently lost because Shadow Copy only works for system files, not user documents

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi government department has a shared folder with 500 subfolders organized by project year. questions.hint: Consider using permission inheritance from the parent folder, with explicit exceptions only where genuinely needed, and auditing existing permissions.

options.text: Reset all subfolders to inherit parent permissions using icacls /reset or GUI inheritance enablement; document and explicitly set only necessary exceptions (e.g., confidential projects); audit with AccessEnum or similar tools to identify and remediate inconsistencies
Manually visit each of the 500 subfolders and rewrite permissions from memory without documentation
Delete all subfolders and recreate them with new permissions, losing all historical project data

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan hospital's patient records system uses a Linux file server with Samba for Windows client access. The administrator sets a folder's Unix permissions to 770. Samba does not use any permission system and all access issues are caused by network cable faults

options.text: Insert Signature Line (with digital certificate from a trusted CA) and optionally apply Document Protection with Restrict Editing to prevent unauthorized modifications

Use WordArt to create a decorative signature graphic that looks professional but offers no security

Convert the document to a plain text file, losing all formatting and visual elements

options.text: Result is 30000; if B3 is deleted, the formula adjusts to =SUM(B2:B4) and excludes the deleted cell, resulting in 15000
Result is 30000; if B3 is deleted, the formula returns a #REF! error because the range is broken
Result is 300000 because Excel multiplies by 10 for budget calculations
Result is 0 because SUM only works with text values, not numbers

options.text: 15, because the formula always uses 0.10 regardless of the condition
150, because the IF function returns the condition value, not the calculation result
0.15, because Excel returns the rate multiplier rather than the computed charge

Conditional Formatting, which only changes cell appearance based on values but does not restrict input
Cell Protection, which prevents editing but does not restrict values to a specific list
Formula Auditing, which traces formula dependencies but does not validate data entry

questions.text: Scenario: A Nakuru county office tracks employee attendance in Excel. Column A has dates, Column B has employee names, Column C has 'Present' or 'Absent'. The HR manager wants to count how many times 'John Kamau' was 'Present'. Which function combination achieves this?

options.text: COUNTIFS(B:B, 'John Kamau', C:C, 'Present'), which counts rows where both conditions are met simultaneously

=500000/5, which ignores salvage value and yields 100000 KES per year

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan university's finance department uses Excel to project student fee revenue. The formula =PMT(0.05/12, 24, -100000) is used. What does this formula calculate and what is the approximate result?
questions.hint: PMT calculates periodic loan payments. The rate is 5% annual divided by 12 months, 24 periods, present value 100000.

The total interest paid over 24 months, approximately 10000 KES
The future value of 100000 KES after 24 months at 5% interest, approximately 110000 KES
The number of months required to pay off 100000 KES at 4387 KES per month, which is 24

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi government department maintains a 5000-row Excel database of contractor payments. questions.hint: Consider conditional formatting for visual identification, Remove Duplicates for data cleaning, and advanced filtering for non-destructive analysis.

options.text: Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cell Rules > Duplicate Values to visually identify duplicates; Remove Duplicates (Data tab) to create a clean copy while preserving original; or Advanced Filter to extract unique records to a new location without modifying source data
Manually scroll through all 5000 rows and delete rows that look similar
Sort by contractor name and delete every other row assuming alternation
Use Find and Replace to replace all contractor names with 'DUPLICATE'

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan hospital's procurement department uses Excel to track medical supply orders across 12 months. options.text: Pivot Table to aggregate spending by category and month; Pivot Chart to visualize trends; Conditional Formatting to highlight cells exceeding budget thresholds; SUMIFS formulas for real-time budget comparison calculations
WordArt for decorative titles and Clip Art for medical supply images
A single large table with 500 columns, one per order, manually colored with fill colors
Print the spreadsheet and pin it to a physical bulletin board for visual monitoring

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi financial services firm uses Excel workbooks linked to external SQL databases for real-time trading data. The workbooks contain complex VBA macros, array formulas, and Power Query connections. Performance has degraded to the point where recalculation takes 15 minutes. Analyze the technical bottlenecks: what combination of factors causes this slowdown and what optimization strategy addresses each?
questions.hint: Consider volatile functions, full-column references, array formula overhead, external query refresh frequency, and VBA event triggers.

options.text: Volatile functions (NOW, RAND, INDIRECT) trigger full recalculation; full-column references (A:A) force evaluation of millions of cells; array formulas process large ranges; frequent external queries block calculation; VBA event handlers fire on every change. Optimization: replace volatile functions with static values, use specific ranges, convert array formulas to helper columns, schedule query refresh, and disable unnecessary events
The computer needs more RAM; simply add 64GB and the problem will be solved
Excel is inherently slow and the firm should switch to manual ledger books
Delete all formulas and type calculated values directly into cells

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi county office replaces all desktop computers with thin clients connecting to a central terminal server. Which component is eliminated at the workstation level compared to traditional fat clients?
questions.hint: Consider the primary storage and processing components that thin clients outsource to the central server.

options.text: Local hard disk drives and extensive RAM, as processing and storage are centralized on the terminal server
Network interface cards, which are still required for server connectivity
Keyboards and mice, which are replaced by touchscreens in all thin client implementations
Operating systems, which are still present as embedded thin client OS firmware

questions.hint: Identify the Microsoft server technology that provides directory services, authentication, and policy enforcement for Windows networks.

Microsoft Office 365, which is a cloud productivity suite without network management capabilities
Windows Defender, which is an antivirus tool and does not manage user accounts

questions.hint: Consider the Windows Update feature that allows organizations to define maintenance windows and defer automatic restarts.

Task Manager, which only monitors running processes and cannot schedule updates

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi law firm uses a RAID 1 array on their file server for document storage. One drive fails on a Friday evening. The IT technician is unavailable until Monday. What is the firm's data availability status during this period?
questions.hint: Consider RAID 1's mirroring architecture and whether a single drive failure causes data unavailability or degraded performance.

options.text: Data remains fully available because RAID 1 mirrors data across two drives; the surviving drive continues serving all requests, though without redundancy until the failed drive is replaced
All data is immediately lost because RAID 1 requires both drives to reconstruct any file
The server crashes and remains offline until the technician replaces the failed drive
Only half the files are accessible, specifically those stored on the surviving drive

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan government agency's mixed OS environment (Windows 10, Ubuntu Linux, macOS) shares files via a central Samba server. Users report intermittent access issues where Windows clients can connect but Linux clients receive 'Permission Denied' errors. Analyze the multi-layered permission architecture causing this inconsistency.
questions.hint: Consider Samba's user mapping, Unix permissions, SELinux contexts, and how different clients authenticate differently.

options.text: Samba maps Windows users to Unix users; if mapping fails, Linux clients may authenticate as 'nobody'; Unix permissions (770) may exclude mapped users; SELinux may block Samba access to the share path; all layers must be verified for consistent cross-platform access
Linux clients are inherently incompatible with Samba and should use NFS exclusively
The permission denied error is caused by network cable faults, not configuration issues
Windows and Linux use identical authentication mechanisms, so the issue must be hardware-related

questions.hint: Consider how explicit permission settings on child objects override inherited permissions from the parent.

options.text: Managers have no access because inheritance was removed and they were not explicitly granted permissions in the subfolder
Managers retain Modify access through hidden administrator privileges that override explicit settings
Managers retain Modify access because parent permissions always propagate regardless of inheritance settings
Managers have Full Control because they created the subfolder and are the owner

options.text: New files created in the directory inherit the directory's group ownership, ensuring medical staff can access files regardless of the creator's primary group
The directory becomes executable by all group members, allowing them to run programs inside it
The directory is encrypted and can only be accessed by the group owner
All existing files in the directory are renamed with the group prefix

Which tool automates this bulk permission application?
questions.hint: Identify the command-line utility that modifies ACLs on files and folders recursively, supporting bulk operations.

options.text: icacls with the /grant and /t (traverse) switches, which applies permissions recursively through folder hierarchies
Notepad, which can edit text files but cannot modify file system permissions
Microsoft Paint, which is an image editing tool unrelated to permissions

options.text: Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) combined with proper share permissions; or enabling 'Check Out' document management in SharePoint/OneDrive; or using Excel's Co-Authoring in SharePoint Online which merges changes rather than overwriting
The Recycle Bin, which only stores deleted files, not overwritten content

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi financial firm has a complex permission structure on their file server: 50 shared folders, 200 user accounts, 15 security groups. Delete all user accounts and recreate them from scratch, losing all profile data
Grant Everyone Full Control to simplify the permission structure and eliminate audit findings

Continue generating transcripts and fix errors only when students complain

questions.text: Scenario: A Nairobi NGO's 120-page annual report must be converted to PDF for distribution. The document contains hyperlinks, bookmarks, and embedded fonts. Which PDF export settings ensure the hyperlinks remain active and fonts are embedded for universal viewing?

questions.text: Scenario: A Kenyan university's legal affairs office manages 300 active legal cases using Word documents.
